walkthrough:
What the pat Gene Actually Does**
The pat gene from Streptomyces makes phosphinothricin N-acetyltransferase. That enzyme stops the action of glufosinate. So the soybean plant itself is not harmed when the herbicide is sprayed.

Why Spraying Helps the Crop**
Glufosinate still kills normal plants, so weeds in the same field are killed. With weeds removed, there is much less competition between weeds and soybean for light for photosynthesis, water for growth, and mineral ions such as nitrates and magnesium from the soil.

Link to More Food**
Less competition means more soybean plants survive and grow well to harvest. That gives a higher yield per hectare, so more food can be produced from the same land to help meet global demand.

Final answer: LibertyLink soybean is resistant to / not killed by the herbicide glufosinate. The herbicide kills weeds / unwanted plants. This reduces competition for light, water and soil minerals. More crop survives so higher yield is harvested, helping meet food demand.

hints: Think of the tool that cuts DNA at a specific base sequence to isolate a gene from donor DNA.
walkthrough:
Cutting Out a Specific Gene**
To get the pat gene out of S. viridochromogenes DNA you need an enzyme that cuts DNA at a specific recognition sequence. That is a restriction enzyme, also called a restriction endonuclease.
Final answer: Restriction enzyme / restriction endonuclease.

hints: Think of the enzyme that seals DNA fragments together by rebuilding the sugar-phosphate backbone.
walkthrough:
Joining DNA Back Together**
After cutting, the pat gene and the opened plasmid must be joined by forming new phosphodiester bonds in the backbone. The enzyme that seals nicks and joins fragments is DNA ligase.

walkthrough:
Growing Needs the Right Environment**
Using a product in food only needs import and processing. Growing needs suitable temperature, rainfall and soil for soybean, plus enough available farmland. Many of the other 15 countries may simply have an unsuitable climate or no spare land.

Laws and Attitudes to GM**
Growing GM crops often needs separate government approval from eating imported GM food. Some countries may have banned cultivation of GM LibertyLink soybean or face strong opposition from activist groups and consumers, even if they allow the imported product.

The Herbicide May Be the Problem**
The advantage only works if farmers can spray glufosinate. If a country has banned glufosinate for health or environmental reasons, there is no benefit in growing the resistant variety there.

Final answer: Any three from: other countries may have unsuitable climate / soil for soybean; may lack regulatory approval / have banned growing GM crops; may have opposition from pressure groups / public to growing GM; may lack available land; may have banned use of glufosinate herbicide.
